name: Gerrit Code Review
summary: A self-hosted Git server built around code review: every commit is pushed for review first, reviewers vote on it, and only an approved change is merged into the branch. Android and Chromium use it.
intro: Gerrit is a Java server that hosts Git repositories and puts a review step in front of every branch. Developers don’t push to `main`; they push to the special ref `refs/for/main`, and Gerrit turns each new commit into a change waiting for review. A `commit-msg` hook adds a `Change-Id:` line to every commit message. To address comments you amend the commit, keep that line, and push again: Gerrit adds the new version to the same change as another patch set, so the review keeps its history across amends and rebases.

Reviewers comment on diffs and vote on labels. By default Code-Review runs from −2 (“must not be submitted”, a veto) to +2 (approved), and the default submit requirement is at least one +2 and no −2; projects often add a Verified label, from −1 (build or tests failed) to +1. The unit of review is a single commit, not a branch, so a large piece of work becomes a chain of small dependent changes, each reviewed and updated on its own. Since Gerrit 3.0 (May 2019) changes, comments, accounts and groups are stored in Git itself, in a format called NoteDb, instead of a separate SQL database.

The Android Open Source Project reviews all its code in Gerrit (uploads go through `repo upload`), and so does Chromium (through `git cl upload`). A new minor version ships about every six months: 3.13.0 on November 10, 2025 and 3.14.0 on May 15, 2026, with 3.14.4 the latest in September 2026 and 3.15.0 planned for November 13, 2026. Version 3.14 turned on Review Agent, AI-assisted review, by default whenever a plugin providing an AI review model is installed; private changes are not shared with it.
strengths: Review is enforced by the server, not by convention: changes reach a branch only through submit rules such as one +2, no −2 and a passing Verified vote
Reviews single commits, so big work can land as a chain of small changes, each reviewed and amended separately with its full patch-set history
Proven at very large scale on projects such as Android and Chromium, which run their own public Gerrit instances
Free software under Apache 2.0, and since 3.0 the review data lives in Git repositories rather than a separate database
limits: An unfamiliar workflow for people used to pull requests: install a commit hook, push to `refs/for/…`, and amend commits instead of adding fix-up commits
A review server, not a whole forge: there is no issue tracker or CI built in, so those come from separate tools
You run it yourself, and some upgrades need a full reindex (3.14 moved the changes index from version 87 to 88)
Only the newest minor versions are supported: 3.11 reached end of life when 3.14 shipped, so staying supported means upgrading about once a year

snippet.title: Upload a change for review, then a second patch set
source: # once per clone: the hook that adds a Change-Id line to each commit message
git push origin HEAD:refs/for/main               # creates a change for review on main
# reviewer asks for a fix: amend, keep the Change-Id, push again
git push origin HEAD:refs/for/main -o topic=login  # patch set 2 of the same change

story: Gerrit comes from Google’s internal code review. In 2005 Guido van Rossum began Mondrian, a tool for reviewing every change before it was submitted to Google’s central Perforce repository; it depended on Google-only services such as Bigtable, so it could not be released. In 2008 he open-sourced parts of it as Rietveld, which ran on Google App Engine and worked with Subversion. Rietveld was strictly advisory: it did not stop anyone from submitting unreviewed code.

Android had chosen Git, and its engineers wanted something like Mondrian for it. App Engine was a deal-breaker, because the phone makers working on Android keep internal repositories and won’t rely on an outside service. Gerrit started as a set of patches to Rietveld for the Android Open Source Project and became a fork once it added access control that van Rossum did not want in Rietveld’s code. It is named after Gerrit Rietveld, the Dutch architect after whom Rietveld was named. Shawn Pearce, who had reimplemented Git in Java as JGit, led the project, and Gerrit 2.0 (January 2009) was a full rewrite from Python on App Engine to Java with a SQL database. By October 2009 HTC, Qualcomm, TI, Sony Ericsson and Google were running it.

Over the next decade Gerrit moved its data into Git. Pearce told LWN in 2009 that Gerrit not working offline was “a bug” and listed storing metadata in Git as planned work; Gerrit 3.0, in May 2019, removed the old database (“ReviewDb”) for changes, accounts, groups and projects, and dropped the old GWT web interface for the newer PolyGerrit one. Releases now come about every six months, and 3.14 (May 2026) added AI-assisted review as a built-in step.

choices.why: Rietveld only advised; nothing stopped a direct submit. Android’s partners needed control over who could change what, and adding those access-control features is what turned Gerrit from a set of Rietveld patches into a fork.

choices.choice: Review one commit at a time, tracked by a Change-Id
choices.why: A commit’s hash changes every time it is amended or rebased. A Change-Id line in the message stays the same, so Gerrit can recognize a reworked commit as a new patch set of the same change instead of a new review.

choices.choice: Java and JGit instead of the `git` program
choices.why: JGit let the server read and write repositories directly, without starting the C `git` binary for each operation, and most Android developers already worked in Java.
Keeping changes, comments, accounts and groups in Git removed the separate SQL database from the core of a Gerrit server; only a small table of which files each user has reviewed still needs one.
